assess.s: establish what actually broke and pick the recovery path

record_cluster_state.s:
READ-ONLY. Change nothing. This leaf only gathers facts.

SITUATION: Qdrant Cloud cluster `a154ee19-467b-41d1-9fb8-91139b49b0a0` (region `eu-west-2-0.aws`) returns HTTP 503 `no available server` on EVERY data-plane endpoint — `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/collections`, `/telemetry` and `/cluster` all fail identically (verified 2026-08-04). So the REST API is unusable and **the puzzles cannot be deleted with curl until the cluster runs again**. That is circular: the data suspected of filling the disk can only be removed by a cluster that will not start. The only way in is the Qdrant Cloud console at https://cloud.qdrant.io, a separate control plane that stays reachable while the data plane is down. There is no Qdrant Cloud control-plane API key anywhere in `~/i/e4/.env` — only `QDRANT_URL` and `QDRANT_KEY`, which are data-plane credentials — so this is done by hand in the browser.

BLAST RADIUS — four projects share this cluster, confirmed by grepping each repo's `.env` for the cluster id:
`~/i/e4` (collection `i` holds e4's USERS, TOKEN BALANCES and SAVED GAMES, plus the partial `puz`), `~/i/x2`, `~/i/i`, `~/i/me/a8`.
Nothing in this plan may risk collection `i`.

SUSPECTED CAUSE: an ingest of the 6,014,381-row lichess puzzle corpus into a vectorless `puz` collection was interrupted at roughly 2,300,000 rows when the cluster began returning 503. A payload-only ingest that size plausibly exhausted the disk, and a full disk stops Qdrant from starting, taking every collection with it. THIS IS A HYPOTHESIS. Confirm or kill it here.

DO THIS: log in at https://cloud.qdrant.io, open cluster `a154ee19-467b-41d1-9fb8-91139b49b0a0`, and write these into the step notes verbatim: tier/plan (free vs paid), configured disk size in GB, RAM, and the DISK USAGE metric. Disk at or near 100% confirms the hypothesis.

IF DISK IS NOT NEAR FULL: the hypothesis is dead. Deleting `puz` will not revive the cluster. Say so to the user, open a Qdrant support ticket, and note it here — the rest of this plan still applies (puzzles are moving to Cloudflare D1 either way, see `plan/puzzles_d1.plan.json`) but the outage needs a separate diagnosis.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
cloud.qdrant.io -> cluster a154ee19 -> Detail page: read tier, disk size, RAM and the disk-usage % off the page and write all four into the step notes

check_backups_and_choose_path.s:
Decide, on evidence, which recovery path the rest of this plan follows. Record the choice and the reason in the step notes before moving on, and tell the user which one and what it costs.

In the console, open the cluster's **Backups** tab. Qdrant Cloud backups are NOT automatic — they exist only if a schedule was enabled or someone clicked "Backup now". Record whether any backup exists and the exact timestamp of the newest one.

**PATH A — a backup exists that predates the puzzle ingest.** Restore it into a NEW cluster. The restore predates `puz`, so the new cluster comes up clean, at the ORIGINAL disk size, with `i`/`x2`/`a8` intact, and the monthly cost stays flat. The tradeoff: every write made after the backup timestamp is lost. Weigh that against what collection `i` has taken since — new users, token purchases, saved games. If that loss is unacceptable, take path B even though a backup exists.

**PATH B — no usable backup, or the post-backup writes matter.** Scale the existing cluster's disk UP in the console, let it start, delete `puz`. Zero data loss. The cost: Qdrant Cloud documents that disk **cannot be scaled back down** — "it is not possible to scale down the disk space of the cluster due to technical limitations of the underlying cloud providers." Path B therefore raises the monthly floor permanently. If the cluster is on the FREE tier it cannot be scaled at all, so path B becomes "upgrade to paid, then scale".

Write `PATH A` or `PATH B` plus the reason into the notes. Every later leaf that says "PATH A only" or "PATH B only" is skipped accordingly.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
cloud.qdrant.io -> cluster a154ee19 -> Backups tab: the backup list is visible, and PATH A or PATH B is written into the notes with its reason

restore_into_new_cluster.s:
PATH A ONLY — skip entirely and mark done if `assess.check_backups_and_choose_path` chose PATH B.

1. Console -> cluster `a154ee19…` -> Backups -> select the chosen backup -> Restore -> **into a new cluster**. Do NOT restore over the existing cluster; leaving the broken one untouched preserves the fallback.
2. Wait for the new cluster to report healthy in the console.
3. Copy its new URL and create an API key for it. Keep both to hand — `purge` and `repoint` need them.
4. Confirm from a shell, substituting the new values:
   `curl -s -m 15 -H "api-key: <new key>" "<new url>/healthz"`
   It must return a real health response, not `no available server`.
5. Do NOT repoint any app yet. That is the `repoint` group, and only after the collections are verified.
6. Write the new URL into the step notes. Until `repoint` runs, `~/i/e4/.env` still points at the OLD cluster, so any leaf below that sources `.env` must be run with the new values substituted by hand.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
cloud.qdrant.io: the newly restored cluster shows status healthy, and its URL is recorded

scale_disk_up.s:
PATH B ONLY — skip entirely and mark done if `assess.check_backups_and_choose_path` chose PATH A.

1. Console -> cluster `a154ee19…` -> Scale / Configuration. Raise **DISK ONLY**. Leave RAM and CPU alone — the failure is storage, and RAM/CPU cost more per GB. Add enough headroom for the partial `puz` collection plus working room; roughly double the current disk size.
2. Apply and wait for the cluster to report healthy. This can take several minutes and may restart nodes.
3. Record the new disk size and the new monthly cost in the step notes, and TELL THE USER this is not reversible — Qdrant Cloud cannot shrink a disk.

IF the cluster reports healthy in the console but the data plane still returns `no available server`: STOP. Disk was not the cause. Do not proceed to deletion. Open a Qdrant support ticket and tell the user.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
cloud.qdrant.io: cluster a154ee19 shows the raised disk size and status healthy

confirm_data_plane_live.s:
Prove the cluster actually serves requests again before anything destructive happens.

PATH B: `source ~/i/e4/.env && curl -s -m 15 -H "api-key: $QDRANT_KEY" "$QDRANT_URL/healthz"` must return a real health response over HTTP 200.
PATH A: same call with the NEW cluster's URL and key from `recover.restore_into_new_cluster`.

Then confirm `/collections` lists collections instead of erroring. If either still 503s, this leaf is not done — go back to the recover leaf for your path.

purge.s: remove every puzzle that reached qdrant

inventory_before_delete.s:
The cluster is reachable. Take a full inventory BEFORE deleting anything, so the deletion is provably scoped to puzzles and there is a before-picture to verify against.

PATH A: substitute the new cluster's URL/key everywhere below; `.env` is not repointed yet.

source ~/i/e4/.env
curl -s -H "api-key: $QDRANT_KEY" "$QDRANT_URL/collections" | python3 -m json.tool

Then record every collection's point count:

for c in $(curl -s -H "api-key: $QDRANT_KEY" "$QDRANT_URL/collections" | python3 -c "import json,sys; [print(x['name']) for x in json.load(sys.stdin)['result']['collections']]"); do
  printf "%-16s " "$c"
  curl -s -H "api-key: $QDRANT_KEY" "$QDRANT_URL/collections/$c" | python3 -c "import json,sys; r=json.load(sys.stdin)['result']; print('points', r.get('points_count'), '| status', r.get('status'))"
done

Paste that output into the step notes. It is the before-picture for `purge.verify_shared_collections_intact`.

SANITY CHECK: confirm `puz` really is the puzzle collection and really is large.
curl -s -H "api-key: $QDRANT_KEY" "$QDRANT_URL/collections/puz" | python3 -m json.tool
Expect a point count near 2,300,000 (where the ingest was interrupted) and payload indexes `t` (keyword), `r` (integer), `v` (integer) — the ones the ingest created. If the count is tiny, or `puz` does not exist, then little or nothing was written and the outage had another cause: say so to the user, and mark `purge.delete_puz_collection` done without running the DELETE.

delete_puz_collection.s:
Delete the puzzle data. Dropping the whole collection is correct and is exactly what the user asked for: `puz` contains ONLY lichess puzzles, and it is being replaced by Cloudflare D1 (`plan/puzzles_d1.plan.json`). Dropping the collection is cleaner and far faster than deleting points, and it releases the payload indexes too.

IRREVERSIBLE. `purge.inventory_before_delete` must be recorded first and the user must have been told. Never run this against any other collection name — in particular never against `i`, which holds e4's users, token balances and saved games.

PATH A: substitute the new cluster's URL/key.

source ~/i/e4/.env
curl -s -X DELETE -H "api-key: $QDRANT_KEY" "$QDRANT_URL/collections/puz"

Expect exactly `{"result":true,"status":"ok","time":…}`.

Then watch the disk usage metric fall in the Qdrant Cloud console — it can take a few minutes as segments are reclaimed. Record the before and after numbers in the step notes.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
cloud.qdrant.io: the cluster disk-usage metric has visibly dropped from the number recorded before the delete

verify_shared_collections_intact.s:
Prove e4's own user data and the other three projects survived. This is the leaf that catches a mistake while it is still fixable.

1. Compare against the inventory from `purge.inventory_before_delete`. Every collection except `puz` must still exist with the SAME point count.
2. Collection `i` carries e4's users, token balances and saved games, multi-tenanted by payload field `s`. Spot-check a real read:
   source ~/i/e4/.env
   curl -s -X POST -H "api-key: $QDRANT_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"filter":{"must":[{"key":"s","match":{"value":"u"}}]},"limit":3,"with_payload":true}' "$QDRANT_URL/collections/i/points/scroll" | python3 -m json.tool
   Expect user points carrying `s: 'u'` and an `e` (email) field.
3. Exercise `~/i/x2`, `~/i/i` and `~/i/me/a8` against the cluster at least once each — a real read, not a ping. Their `.env` files all carry this same cluster id.
4. PATH A: all of the above runs against the NEW cluster.

If any non-`puz` collection is missing or short, STOP and tell the user immediately — on PATH A the old cluster is still intact and is the fallback.

repoint.s: move all four apps onto the recovered cluster (PATH A only)

update_env_and_secrets.s:
PATH A ONLY — skip entirely and mark done on PATH B, which keeps the same URL and key.

The restore produced a new cluster with a new URL and key. All four projects must move or they keep hitting the dead cluster.

For each of `~/i/e4`, `~/i/x2`, `~/i/i`, `~/i/me/a8`:
1. Update `QDRANT_URL` and `QDRANT_KEY` in that repo's `.env`. Repo rule: local env vars ALWAYS live in `.env`, never `.dev.vars` — delete a `.dev.vars` if you find one.
2. Update the DEPLOYED secrets too, or production keeps failing while local works. For Cloudflare Workers projects those are declared in `wrangler.toml`/`wrangler.jsonc`. Read secrets only through `$env/dynamic/private` and the repo's `get_secret` / `SecretVal` abstraction — never reintroduce a raw `env.KEY` read.
3. Redeploy.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
each of the four deployed apps (e4, x2, i, a8) performs a real Qdrant-backed read against the new cluster

retire_old_cluster.s:
PATH A ONLY — skip and mark done on PATH B.

Only after every app is verified green on the new cluster: delete the old broken cluster `a154ee19-467b-41d1-9fb8-91139b49b0a0` in the Qdrant Cloud console so it stops costing money. Update the cluster id anywhere it is documented (`AGENTS.md` files across the four repos, any notes). Record the new cluster id in `~/i/e4/AGENTS.md`.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
cloud.qdrant.io: cluster a154ee19 no longer appears in the cluster list

retire_qdrant_ingest_script.s: `git rm scripts/ingest_puzzles.mjs` in `~/i/e4` — the Qdrant puzzle ingest is superseded by `scripts/build_puzzles.mjs` (Cloudflare D1). If `plan/puzzles_d1.plan.json` already removed it, confirm it is gone and mark this done. Commit scoped to this step.

document_shared_cluster_rule.s:
Root cause was not a bad query. It was putting one app's bulk, regenerable, read-only dataset onto the cluster that serves every other production app, with no size ceiling.

Add to `~/i/e4/AGENTS.md` under Architecture:
- The Qdrant cluster is SHARED by e4, x2, i and a8. Collection `i` holds e4's users, token balances and saved games. Never bulk-load a large regenerable dataset onto it — a ~2.3M-row puzzle ingest filled its disk on 2026-08-04 and took every collection on the cluster down with it, and Qdrant Cloud disk cannot be scaled back down afterwards. Bulk read-only data belongs in Cloudflare D1.

Commit scoped to this step.
document_shared_cluster_rule.t: bash -c 'grep -q "SHARED by e4, x2, i and a8" ~/i/e4/AGENTS.md'

enable_automatic_backups.s:
The single highest-value item in this plan. Do not skip it.

Backups were OFF, which is why this outage had no clean recovery path. In the Qdrant Cloud console, on the LIVE cluster (the new one on PATH A, the scaled one on PATH B): Backups tab -> enable a schedule -> daily. Then click "Backup now" and wait for the first backup to complete, so a recovery point exists today rather than tomorrow.

Also add a disk-usage alert if the plan offers one.

Record in the step notes: schedule enabled, and the timestamp of the first completed backup.

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
cloud.qdrant.io -> live cluster -> Backups: a daily schedule is enabled and at least one completed backup is listed

unblock.s:
finish the work this outage blocked

BROWSER CHECK (was an unverified "b" gate — confirm it by hand or turn it into an agent-browser grep):
e4 loads and a logged-in user sees their saved game and their token balance

run_legacy_user_migration.s:
`plan/sso.plan.json` step `migrate_legacy_e4_records` was blocked by this outage. The implementor reported: `scripts/migrate_legacy_users.mjs` is written and committed as `7e844d3`, is idempotent (moves `u_`-prefixed points to unprefixed ids and backfills `e` and `pic`), and its 4 unit tests pass — but the live run could not execute because the cluster returned 503.

Run it now against the recovered cluster. Then verify the migration actually landed by scrolling collection `i` for any remaining `u_`-prefixed point ids — there must be none. It is idempotent, so re-running after a partial run is safe.

Then mark `migrate_legacy_e4_records` done in `plan/sso.plan.json` with that plan's own mark command, and commit scoped to it.

rerun_e4_gate.s:
Re-run e4's full gate: `pnpm test`, `pnpm type-check`, `pnpm check`.

Do NOT confuse two different failure sets. `plan/puzzles_d1.plan.json` is separately repairing 23 stale test failures in `config.test.ts`, `pieces.test.ts` and `learn.e2e.test.ts` — those are static string-matching assertions and have nothing to do with the outage. What this leaf cares about is that no NETWORK-related failure remains.

Finally, tell the user plainly which of the two plans is now unblocked and what is left in each.
